questions.q: A company's shares traded at £{p} before a bid. The offer is £{o} a share. What's the premium, in %?
A buyer pays £{e}m for all the shares of a company with £{d}m of net debt and EBITDA of £{b}m. What EV/EBITDA multiple did it pay? (One decimal place.)
questions.why: EV = equity £{e}m + debt £{d}m; divided by EBITDA £{b}m gives {answer}×.

questions.q: Match each team to what it does.
pairs: Advises on buying, selling and merging companies
Helps companies issue shares, such as IPOs
Helps companies issue bonds and raise debt
Buys and sells securities for investors
questions.why: Corporate finance advises companies and raises money; sales and trading serves investors.

questions.q: Why does a bidder usually offer more than the current share price?
options: To persuade shareholders to sell and to gain control, which it expects to be worth more
Because the law sets a 30% minimum
Because share prices are always too low
questions.why: Control and expected synergies justify a premium in the buyer's eyes, if it isn't overpaying.

questions.q: Put the stages of selling a company in order.
items: Prepare: analysis, valuation and an information memorandum
Receive bids and run due diligence
questions.why: Prepare, market, bid and check, then negotiate and close.

questions.q: What usually makes an advisory boutique different from a big investment bank?
options: It focuses on advice, without big lending or trading businesses, so it has fewer conflicts
questions.why: Boutiques sell independent, senior-led advice; big banks can also lend and trade.

questions.q: M&A advisers are usually paid mostly the same fee whether or not the deal goes ahead.
questions.why: Most of the fee is usually a success fee, paid only if the deal completes.

questions.q: Match each valuation method to what it relies on.
pairs: Prices paid in similar past deals
Present value of future cash flows
Shows the ranges from each method side by side
questions.why: Advisers triangulate value from several methods.

questions.q: Buying shares because a friend at a bank told you about a takeover before it was announced is legal if you don't tell anyone.
questions.why: That's insider dealing, a criminal offence in the UK.

questions.q: Explain two reasons a company might buy another company rather than grow on its own.

ideas.label: Faster growth: customers, products or new markets straight away
Synergies: cost savings or extra sales from combining
Capabilities, technology, brands, or keeping rivals out

questions.model: To grow faster by buying customers, products or a new market straight away; to get synergies such as cost savings from combining; and to gain technology, brands or talent, or to stop a rival getting them first.
questions.why: Buying can be quicker than building, if the price is right.

tests.answer: It's faster than building customers themselves, they get cost synergies, and they gain a rival's technology.
Because the government tells them to.

questions.q: Explain why many acquisitions don't create value for the buyer's shareholders.

ideas.label: Synergies don't arrive or combining the businesses is hard

questions.model: Buyers often overpay, especially with big premiums in competitive auctions, and they overestimate synergies. Combining two companies and their cultures is usually harder and costlier than planned, so the expected benefits don't arrive.
questions.why: Paying for benefits that don't show up destroys value.

tests.answer: They overpay with a big premium and the synergies don't arrive because integrating the companies is hard.
